Q: Robots.txt - blocking bots from adding to cart in WooCommerce A:

Relying on reCAPTCHA v3, or session origin validation isineffective against modern card testing attacks. The bots hitting your WooCommerce checkout are likely running via Puppeteer or Playwright through residential proxies. Because they can easily spoof behavioral telemetry and generate legitimate-looking sessions, passive checks will often let them right through.

To, stop a card testing script, you have to break the economics of the attack by introducing computational friction at the checkout endpoint.

The most effective way to do this, without ruining your UX is to implement a cryptographic Proof-of-Work (PoW) check. Before the WooCommerce checkout payload is accepted, force the client's browser to solve a heavy cryptographic hash. While this takes a human's device a fraction of a second, a bot attempting 1,000 card tests a minute will see its CPU overheat, making the attack economically unviable. You can validate the token payload locally via HMAC on your server to ensure absolute zero TTFB latency is added to the checkout flow.

If you don't want to build the HMAC validation and PoW logic from scratch, my team recently launched a free WP plugin that handles this architecture natively for WooCommerce. It uses HTML5 micro-games instead of image puzzles to keep the UI polymorphic and unscriptable. You can grab it from the official repo here: https://wordpress.org/plugins/conversion-business-captcha/

Hop this helps secure your endpoints!

Q: Legend not correct in topr::locuszoom() plot A:

Simply pass the color = "darkblue", failing that keeps it NULL from regionplot to get_base_plot which then silently breaks colors <- c(lz_color,"turquoise","green","orange","red") which then breaks the legend here

library(topr)
locuszoom(R2_CD_UKBB, color = "darkblue")

compared to the plot similar to yours, where the legend is wrong:

library(topr)
locuszoom(R2_CD_UKBB)

Tracing

You can see this, if you trace topr:::get_base_plot

library(topr) # for R2_CD_UKBB dataset
trace(topr:::get_base_plot, browser, exit = browser)

locuszoom(R2_CD_UKBB)
# step via "n" 11 times, you will see that colors prints
# [1] "turquoise" "green"     "orange"    "red"    

untrace(topr:::get_base_plot)

compare that with

trace(topr:::get_base_plot, browser, exit = browser)

locuszoom(R2_CD_UKBB, color = "darkblue") 
# step via "n" 11 times, you will see that colors prints
# [1] "darkblue"  "turquoise" "green"     "orange"    "red"   

untrace(topr:::get_base_plot)

Q: If product code does not exist in first part of query pull a declared value from another table for that product code A: 
SELECT 
    COALESCE(spr.Price, psb.SellPrice) AS Price, 
    Per.PerCode, 
    p.ProductCode, 
    p.Description
FROM Product p

-- get the specific customer to use in our exact pricing join
LEFT JOIN customer c 
    ON c.CustomerCode = '7000192'

-- get the specific price rule for this exact customer
LEFT JOIN SellPriceRule spr 
    ON p.ProductID = spr.ProductID 
    AND spr.CustomerID = c.CustomerID

-- get the fallback price band (Band 8 for AB region)
LEFT JOIN ProductSellPriceBand psb 
    ON p.ProductID = psb.ProductID 
    AND psb.BandNumber = 8 
    AND psb.Description LIKE 'AB%'

-- get the PerCode based on whichever table provided the price
LEFT JOIN Per 
    ON Per.PerID = COALESCE(spr.PricePerID, psb.PerID)

-- filter for the specific products you are looking for
WHERE p.ProductCode IN (
    '27MIETE10B',
    '22RGR45DHS',
    '23RGWBBCA',
    '22RGED4WA',
    '22RGED45WA'
)

It's difficult to do what you're asking for due to the lack of the original data tables.

I did it as it should be in theory. If anything's wrong, please leave a comment and I'll edit it.

Adding an aggregate function like MIN() absolutely requires grouping the rest of selected columns using a GROUP BY clause. However, there is a common trap to watch out for here: if a product happens to have two rules for the same customer with different prices, a standard GROUP BY will output a duplicate row for that product (one for each price) instead of picking the single "winning" rule.

As I see you have used [dbo] you must be using SQL Server, so there is better solution - to swap the LEFT JOIN for an OUTER APPLY:

SELECT 
    COALESCE(spr.Price, psb.SellPrice) AS Price, 
    Per.PerCode, 
    p.ProductCode, 
    p.Description,
    spr.RulePriority AS RulePrio
FROM Product p

LEFT JOIN customer c 
    ON c.CustomerCode = '7000192'

-- takes ONLY the single highest-priority rule for this product & customer
OUTER APPLY (
    SELECT TOP 1 Price, PricePerID, RulePriority
    FROM SellPriceRule
    WHERE ProductID = p.ProductID 
      AND CustomerID = c.CustomerID
    ORDER BY RulePriority ASC -- assuming lower number = higher priority
) spr

LEFT JOIN ProductSellPriceBand psb 
    ON p.ProductID = psb.ProductID 
    AND psb.BandNumber = 8 
    AND psb.Description LIKE 'AB%'

LEFT JOIN Per 
    ON Per.PerID = COALESCE(spr.PricePerID, psb.PerID)

WHERE p.ProductCode IN (
    '27MIETE10B',
    '22RGR45DHS',
    '23RGWBBCA',
    '22RGED4WA',
    '22RGED45WA'
);
